doc.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001

title: Drums, Ben Franklin High School and becoming a left-handed bassist
summary: Crowded drum class sends May to the bass class; he plays left-handed and stays with it, not expecting the career he later had.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: Yeah that was by accident also. Because I always felt that I could see myself up there like a Buddy Rich or a Gene Krupa or some great drummer, with the spotlight on him you know, and all the girls looking at you you know, and that’d be great. So I would take my little allowance you know and go down on 42nd Street, and a Wurlitzer, and take drum lessons on Saturday. And when I got to high school I was going to study the drums. But when I got there — oh Sonny Payne was in that school at that time, and he was like the big, big thing at the Ben Franklin, where a lot of guys went to, like oh there was bunch of us that went there: Sonny Rollins, Jackie McLean. And when I got to the drum class it was so crowded he had students in the hallway. So he says, “Why don’t you go in the bass class?” he grabbed me by my ear. So Walter Bishop was in that class for some reason. It was just the two of us. And he told me — that was when I first met him, too — and he said to me after ten minutes or so of just being in the class waiting for the teacher to come, so he said to me, “Well I don’t know, you got it kid, I’m not going to be in this class.” I was the only one in the bass class. And naturally being left handed, when we had ensemble, you know playing with the orchestra you know, I would play right handed. And when he wouldn’t look I would play left handed. Then he would stop the band — “get on the other side.” So it took me a while before I decided, well I don’t know what side to stand on, I’m more comfortable playing left handed, but I’d never heard of a left handed bass player. But I decided to just stay and make myself comfortable. Because I

had no idea that I would have any kind of career like I’ve had you know. I played with Charlie Parker and Billy Taylor and Miles Davis’ band and I’ve had all kinds of great, wonderful experiences you know, Dizzy Gillespie and all that stuff. So had I thought I probably would have —
Made yourself stay in the band.

Made myself play in there. Because I sort of defeated myself in a little way. Because there’s a lot of things that right handed players can do, I can’t do. Some things. Some technical things. And it would look kind of strange for me to be in a classical orchestra, and everybody else is going this way, it kind of didn’t make much sense.
